titleStmt.title: Dynamic Real-Time Scheduling with Task Migration for Handling Bag-of-Tasks Applications on Clusters

analytic.title: Dynamic Real-Time Scheduling with Task Migration for Handling Bag-of-Tasks Applications on Clusters

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The scheduling of real-time tasks on clusters is a critical issue for offering quality-of-service (QoS) assurance. A significant challenge in real-time task scheduling is to support various types of applications. In this paper we focus on the scheduling of bag-of-tasks (BoT) applications consisting of many independent tasks. BoT applications are a typically "embarrassingly parallel" type of applications which widely exist in various fields in science and engineering. We propose a dynamic (online) real-time scheduling algorithm referred to as scheduling algorithm with migration (SAM) for handling real-time BoT applications on cluster systems. SAM schedules tasks to the minimum number of processors so that computation power can be saved for unscheduled large tasks. SAM also utilizes task migration to optimize load balancing without undermining the schedulability of the tasks. Performance evaluation results are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness and competitiveness of our approaches when compared to existing algorithms.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Clusters have emerged as powerful computing platforms for processing real-time applications. The scheduling of realtime tasks on clusters is a critical issue for providing qualityof-service (QoS) guarantees. One significant challenge in designing real-time scheduling algorithms is to support various types of tasks. In this paper, we focus on Bag-of-Tasks (BoT) applications. BoT applications are a typically "embarrassingly parallel" type of applications consisting of many independent tasks and thus can be processed in parallel without communication or synchronization. Since tasks in a BoT application can be processed on multiple computers concurrently, distributed computer systems are desirable platforms for such applications. A typical example of is the SETI@home [1] project in Berkeley, which exploits desktop grids across the world to perform massive computations. The success of SETI@home spawned many similar projects like Folding@home [2], Rosetta@Home [3], and Einstein@Home [4].

Handling parallel task including BoT applications on distributed computing platforms have wide applicability in scientific and engineering problems such as real-time aircraft tracking [28], real-time simulations [29], and robot arm dynamics [30]. For instance, the robot arm dynamics problem consists of two modules: the computation of dynamics and the solution of linear equations. Both modules have real-time constraints and exhibit high degree of parallelism.

Prior works have widely investigated real-time task scheduling problems on clusters for various types of parallel tasks including task graphs, [10], [11], [12], malleable tasks [13], [14], [15], and arbitrarily divisible loads [19], [20], [21], [22], respectively. However, the scheduling of real-time BoT applications has been neglected in prior works. In this paper we investigate the problem of scheduling real-time BoT applications in distributed computing environments. We contribute a scheduling algorithm referred to as scheduling algorithm with migration (SAM). SAM schedules tasks to the minimum number of processors so that computation power can be saved for unscheduled large tasks. Task migration is then applied to optimize load balancing without undermining the schedulability of all tasks.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 discusses related works. Section 3 introduces mathematical models, assumptions, and problem formulation. Section 4 describes the proposed SAM algorithm in great detail. Section 5 presents simulation results to evaluate the SAM algorithm, with conclusions following in Section 6.

div.head: II. RELATED WORKS
div.p: Real-time scheduling algorithms generally fall into two categories: static (off-line) [10], [11] and dynamic (on-line) [5], [14], [15]. In static algorithms, the allocation of tasks to processors and the times when the tasks start running are determined beforehand. Static algorithms [10] can be applied to schedule periodic real-time tasks and the benefit is that once a schedule is determined, deadlines will never be missed. However, static algorithms cannot be utilized to handle aperiodic real-time tasks whose arrivals are unexpected. Scheduling such tasks requires dynamic algorithms which dynamically admit and schedule new tasks without compromising the guarantees for previously admitted tasks. It was shown that no optimal solutions exist for scheduling aperiodic realtime tasks of which characteristics are unknown beforehand in multiprocessors [8], [6]. Given the hardness of dynamic real-time scheduling on multiprocessor systems, many prior works [5], [14], [15], [19] resorted to heuristic algorithms instead of approximation algorithms. In this paper we will focus on dynamic scheduling of BoT tasks and design an efficient heuristic algorithm.
In the past decades, most prior works on real-time task 978-1-4673-4523-1/12/$31.00 ©2012 IEEE ICON 2012

scheduling in multiprocessors assumed that a task is indivisible (or independent) and computed on only one processor [5], [7], [9]. In recent years, researchers have begun to investigate realtime scheduling of parallel tasks, including both modularly divisible and arbitrarily divisible tasks. Modularly divisible tasks are modeled as either task graphs or malleable tasks. Many real-time heuristic algorithms for scheduling task graphs have been proposed in the literature, especially for off-line scheduling [10], [11], [12]. Xu and Parnas [10] studied realtime scheduling for task graphs with resources and deadline constraints. [11] investigated the scheduling of periodic tasks with precedence constraints. Several recent strategies have also been proposed to deal with the malleable realtime task scheduling problem [13], [14], [15]. The authors in [13] designed real-time algorithms for scheduling tasks on a partitionable hypercube multiprocessor. Another work [14] provided a heuristic for scheduling real-time malleable tasks on multiprocessors. This heuristic assigns a task to multiple processors when the allocation of one processor cannot satisfy the deadline. The authors in [15] designed another heuristic algorithm wherein the number of processors assigned to each task is minimized while the deadline constraints are met.

The scheduling of arbitrarily divisible tasks has received much attention in last twenty years, resulting in a cohesive theory named Divisible Load Theory (DLT) [18]. Several recent algorithms have also been proposed for scheduling realtime divisible tasks in clusters. Lin et al. [19] proposed a real-time divisible load scheduling algorithm which utilizes the DLT rule [18] to compute the minimum number of processors required to satisfy a task's deadline. In another work [20] Lin et al. accommodated different processor available times and designed a real-time divisible load scheduling heuristic that can make use of inserted idle times. Chuprat and Baruah [21] extended the work in [20] and offered exact solutions to improve the approximation solutions proposed in [20]. In [22] Mamat et al. presented a real-time divisible load scheduling algorithm which offers advance reservations.

In order to take the advantage of distributed computing environments, prior works have proposed scheduling strategies for handling BoT applications. Lee and Zomaya [23] presented two scheduling strategies to tackle computationintensive and data-intensive BoT applications in dynamic Grid environments, respectively. In [26] Anglano and Canonico conducted extensive simulations to evaluate the performance of 5 knowledge-free approaches for scheduling multiple BoT applications on desktop Grids. Another work [25] analyzed the behavior of multiple non-cooperative schedulers for processing BoT applications. The authors in [24] designed fault-aware scheduling policies for processing BoT applications on Grids.

div.head: Losup et al. [27] investigated the performance of several
div.p: BoT scheduling policies in large-scale distributed systems. In addition, they proposed a taxonomy of scheduling policies for BoT applications and introduced a workload model.

div.head: III. PROBLEM FORMULATION
div.p: Our target computing platform is a computer cluster connected via high speed networks. Let M be the number of processing nodes in the system and the processors are denoted as (P 1 , P 2 , • • • , P M ). Each processor P m (m = 1, 2, ..., M ) has a compute speed C m . Following prior works [14], [15], we assume that C m s are fixed as the cluster is a dedicated system for the scheduler to execute the real-time tasks.

We assume a real-time aperiodic task model in which each BoT application (or task) T i arrives at time A i and D i is its absolute deadline. Note that we will use the terms "application" and "task" interchangeably. Each task T i consists of a number of N i sub-tasks (T 1 i , T 2 i , ..., T Ni i ) without inter-task communications or dependencies. Let W j i be the workload (or size), i.e., the amount of computations (e.g., floating point operations) required to compute a sub-task T j i (j = 1, 2, ..., N i ). The total workload (or size) of task T i is simply the sum of the workloads of all its sub-tasks. It takes
div.formula: W j i C m time units to compute T j i .
div.p: Following prior works [23], [17], we assume that the workload of each sub-task is known and all the BoT applications are computation-intensive. That is, the input data transmission is negligible as the sizes of the tasks are small and hence transferring them does not impact much on the completion time.

The scheduler has complete knowledge about the currently active list of tasks, but not about future tasks which have not arrived. When a new task arrives, the scheduler runs an admissibility test to dynamically determine whether it is feasible to schedule the new task without compromising the guarantees for previously admitted tasks. The admissibility test is conducted as follows. The scheduler generates a task list containing the new task and all previously admitted tasks. We assume that each sub-task in a BoT task is non-preemptable, but a whole BoT task can be preempted between executing its successive sub-tasks. Hence the task list contains all BoT tasks which have sub-tasks that have not been started execution. The scheduler then executes SAM to schedule all tasks in the list. Upon the completion of the test, if all tasks can be completed within their respective deadlines, it can generate a new schedule to replace the existing schedule and the new task is accepted. Otherwise, it rejects the new task and maintains the existing schedule.

Finally, we assume that each processor has adequate storage to store and compute any amount of data. When compared to the time taken for computation, the time taken for making scheduling decisions is negligible.

div.head: IV. THE SAM ALGORITHM
div.p: In this section we consider the real-time BoT task scheduling problem and propose the SAM algorithm. In SAM, we use EDF to determine the queuing order of the BoT tasks. However, the EDF rule answers only the "queuing order" question, but it does not determine the processor where each sub-task of the selected BoT task is assigned. To solve the problem of processor assignment, one intuitive policy is to first schedule the sub-task whose earliest completion time over all processors is the largest among all unscheduled sub-tasks and then allocates the sub-task to the processor on which the earliest completion time can be achieved. This classical policy is so-called Max-Min (or Earliest Completion Time (ECT) policy). Although this policy is efficient in general task scheduling where the objective is to minimize the overall processing time, yet in scheduling real-time BoT applications, it may be inefficient. We can immediately realize this via the following example. As shown in Fig. 1, we consider scheduling 2 BOT applications on 3 processors with EDF policy. The computation speed of each processor is 1 data unit per time unit. The compute time of the first application T 1 is depicted in grey color and the compute time of the second application T 2 is depicted in white color. T 1 consists of 6 sub-tasks and the size of each sub-task is 1 data unit; T 2 has only 1 sub-task and the size is 6 units. T 1 's deadline D 1 is 6 and T 2 's deadline D 2 is 7. However, if we schedule T 1 on the minimum number of processors that can meet the deadline (i.e., 1 processor), then T 2 can also be successfully scheduled on another processor, as shown in Fig. 1(b). This example shows that in some cases even if the total amount of available computation times of the processors is greater than the required computation time of a task, yet it is still possible that none of the processors can accommodate the task without violating its deadline. Therefore it is beneficial to use the minimum number of processors for allocating loads so that computation capacity can be reserved for unscheduled large tasks. However, using the minimum number of processors may lead to poor load balancing. For example, in Fig. 1(b), the third processor is idle. Such inefficient resource utilization may reduce the schedulability of future tasks as current tasks may finish late and occupy many CPU times after the future tasks arrive. To this end, we propose to use task migration to optimize load balancing and resource utilization. As shown in 1(c), after scheduling all tasks on the minimum number of processors, task migration can improve load balancing on all 3 processors without undermining the schedulability of all tasks.

To solve the scheduling problem, we design the SAM algorithm, which is shown in Algorithm 1. SAM consists of two steps. In step 1, SAM first allocates loads to the minimum number of processors so that computation power can be reserved to unscheduled large tasks (lines 3-14 in Algorithm 1). Then in step 2 task migration is applied to optimize load balancing (lines 18-25 in Algorithm 1). To schedule a selected task, SAM first schedules the largest sub-task among all unscheduled sub-tasks of the BoT task. SAM allocates the sub-task to the processor on which the latest completion time before the deadline can be achieved. By doing so, computation power can be saved for unscheduled big tasks. This can reduce the cases that even if the total amount of available computation times of the processors is greater than the required computation time of a task, yet it is still possible that none of the processors can accommodate the task without violating its deadline.

However, using the minimum number of processors may lead to poor load balancing, which may reduce the schedulability of future tasks. In this case we use task migration to optimize resource utilization. Once all tasks are successfully scheduled in step 1, task migration will be executed in step 2 to enhance resource utilization. Tasks are rescheduled according to the order that they are scheduled in step 1. For a sub-task allocated on a processor P a , if it can be rescheduled to another processor so that its finish time can be reduced, then SAM reschedules it to a processor P b on which its finish time is minimized. Once the sub-task is migrated to P b , it leaves a time slot on P a . Hence all other sub-tasks which are previously scheduled after the migrated sub-task are now advanced to fill the time slot. SAM repeats this process to migrate tasks to optimize load balancing and resource utilization.

div.head: V. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
div.p: In order to assess the effectiveness of the proposed scheduling policy, we will now present a performance evaluation study, carried out by means of a discrete-event simulator. We compare their performance for a large set of operational scenarios, obtained by combining a set of cluster configurations with a set of application workloads. Our interested metric is acceptance ratio, which is defined as the ratio of the number of tasks found schedulable to the number of tasks arriving for scheduling. To understand the merits of our strategy, we compare it with two baseline algorithms: EDF-Max-Min and EDF-MINP. Both of them adopt EDF for load scheduling. EDF-Max-Min adopts the classical Max-Min algorithm for load allocation, while EDF-MINP utilizes the minimum number of processors so that the processors can finish computing when the deadline is met. Hence EDF-MINP shares the same idea to the parallel task scheduling algorithm in [14] and EDF-OPR-MN in [19].

The initial simulation configurations are set as follows: The number of processing nodes is 50. For each processor the computation speed is uniformly distributed in the range [0.5, 1.5]. We let the task inter-arrival times follow an exponential distribution with a mean of 1/λ and we initially set 1/λ as 5 time units. Let the size of each application be uniformly distributed in the range [150, 450] and let the number of subtasks in each application be uniformly distributed in the range [1,10]. To generate a set of real-time tasks, we let a task's relative deadline (defined as D i -A i ) be uniformly distributed in the range [t 1 i , t 1 i * (1 + R)] where t 1 i is the compute time for the task on one processor (t
div.formula: 1 i = N i j=1 W j i Cm
div.p: ) and R is referred to as laxity parameter, which denotes the urgency of the deadlines. Thus smaller values of R indicate that deadlines are more urgent. The initial value of R is set as 1.

In each of the following experiments we vary one interested parameter while fixing other parameters as their initial values to study the effect of the interested parameters. We first evaluate the influence of the laxity parameter R on our algorithms. To simulate different deadlines we vary R among the range [0.1, 3.2] and Fig. 2(a) depicts the acceptance ratio versus R. Also, we vary 1/λ from 1 to 7 and Fig. 2(b) shows the acceptance ratio versus 1/λ. Further, to evaluate the effect of number of processors, we vary M from 30 to 70 and Fig. 2(c) plots the acceptance ratio versus M . Finally, to evaluate the effect of number of sub-tasks (degree of parallelism) in each BoT application, let the number of sub-tasks in each application be uniformly distributed in the range [1, N a ] and we vary N a from 2 to 32. Fig. 2(d) depicts the acceptance ratio versus N a .

The simulation results in Fig. 2 show that the SAM algorithm significantly outperforms EDF-Max-Min and EDF-MINP. This is because for EDF-Max-Min, in some cases even if the total amount of available computation times of the processors is greater than the required computation time of an indivisible task, yet it is possible none of the processors can accommodate the task without violating its deadline. Although this case happens less for EDF-MINP, yet the resource utilization of EDF-MINP may be low and some future tasks may be rejected as current tasks are finished late. In contrast, SAM can efficiently avoid these drawbacks as we described in Section 4. This explains why the SAM algorithm outperforms EDF-Max-Min and EDF-MINP in Fig. 2.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: In this paper we have studied an important problem of scheduling real-time BoT applications on clusters. We have proposed the SAM algorithm which utilizes task migration to optimize resource utilization. With our design, we have conducted extensive simulation tests to quantify the performance of our algorithm. The simulation results have shown that algorithm is very efficient and task migration can effectively improve the performance. This study is expected to spur further research in one or more of the following directions.

One future direction could be accommodating other task types, such as task graphs or malleable tasks. Applying task migration techniques with the algorithms proposed in prior works such as [14], [15] may be a interesting attempt to further optimize the performance of the algorithms proposed in these works. Another promising continuation of this paper is to take into account data-intensive applications. As one future work, it would be worthwhile to extend SAM to deal with communication costs in such applications.
